evidence.title: When the Pacemaker Goes Rogue: Pacemaker-Induced Tachycardia, Syncope, and Car Crash.
evidence.abstract: A 78-year-old male with a history of ischemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction, severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and a device-related implantable cardioverter defibrillator (DR ICD) was admitted following a road traffic accident due to a sudden loss of control of the vehicle following a syncope. Initial investigations ruled out acute coronary syndrome and did not point to neurological causes. Device interrogation revealed the presence of pacemaker-mediated tachycardia (PMT), but since the episode trigger had been programmed off, it was not possible to determine when they occurred, how long they lasted, or their rate. However, atrial threshold testing promptly provoked a PMT. The induced PMT led to a tachycardia of 130 bpm, causing severe symptomatic hypotension with a mean blood pressure falling below 50 mmHg. This could be easily reproduced several times. Given the patient's severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction and the absence of any overt alternative explanation, the PMT likely triggered the syncope preceding the car accident. Management focused on reprogramming the DR ICD. The most critical adaptation was a mode switch from DDD to DDIR to prevent atrial tracking, effectively terminating PMT episodes. A prolongation of the postventricular atrial refractory period (PVARP) was not possible due to the very slow VA conduction. The follow-up revealed no other episodes of PMT and the patient no longer experiences episodes of presyncope or syncope. This report highlights the potential for PMTs to induce severe hemodynamic instability and syncope, underscoring the importance of meticulous device evaluation.

evidence.title: Takotsubo syndrome in the setting of cardiac pacing: A review of mechanistic and clinical perspectives.
evidence.abstract: Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) is a reversible form of acute cardiac syndrome usually arising in response to various emotional and physical stressors. TTS due to cardiac pacing has been an uncommon phenomenon mostly attributable to a variety of periprocedural conventional stressors including anxiety, pain and low cardiac output. Interestingly, intraventricular mechanical factors might also play a pivotal role in TTS evolution due to cardiac pacing. Notably, this phenomenon may be potentially underdiagnosed due to a variety of factors including atypical symptoms and masked electrocardiographic (ECG) changes potentially suggesting its higher incidence in clinical practice.The present paper aims to focus on mechanistic and clinical implications of TTS due to cardiac pacing procedures including conventional permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and conduction system pacing (CSP) along with a particular emphasis on intraventricular mechanical factors as potential TTS triggers in this context.

evidence.title: Bradycardia-induced transient myocardial dysfunction in 3 dogs.
evidence.abstract: Bradycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is a reversible form of myocardial dysfunction caused by prolonged bradyarrhythmia, most commonly due to high-grade atrioventricular block or sinus node dysfunction. Although bradycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is well recognized in human medicine, it remains underreported in veterinary literature. This case series describes 3 dogs diagnosed with 3rd-degree atrioventricular block that presented with clinical signs including exercise intolerance, syncope, and cardiomegaly. Each dog underwent comprehensive diagnostic evaluation, including physical examination, thoracic radiography, echocardiography, and electrocardiography. Bradycardia-induced transient myocardial dysfunction was suspected, based on the presence of bradyarrhythmia in conjunction with cardiac enlargement and preserved systolic function. All dogs were treated with permanent pacemaker implantation. Postoperative follow-ups documented marked clinical improvement, with resolution of exercise intolerance or syncope. Radiographic and echocardiographic reassessments demonstrated reductions in atrial and ventricular internal dimensions, supporting the reversibility of myocardial remodeling once normal heart rate was restored. No major complications were observed during follow-up periods that ranged from several months to > 4 y. Key clinical message: These findings supported the presence of bradycardia-induced transient myocardial dysfunction in dogs and underscored the importance of recognizing bradyarrhythmia as a potentially reversible cause of cardiomyopathy. Early diagnosis and timely pacemaker implantation can result in substantial clinical and structural cardiac recovery.

evidence.title: Leadless pacemaker tine fracture resulting in device migration to the pulmonary artery: A case report.
evidence.abstract: A 96-year-old woman underwent implantation of a leadless pacemaker (Micra™ AV2; Medtronic, Inc., Minneapolis, MN, USA) for sick sinus syndrome. One month after implantation, pacing failure due to an elevated pacing threshold was observed, and the pacing output was increased. At routine follow-up one year after implantation, recurrent pacing failure was detected. Chest radiography revealed migration of the device into the left pulmonary artery. At least two of the four fixation tines were missing from the device body, and one fractured tine remained embedded in the right ventricular myocardium. Because the patient was asymptomatic, ventricular pacing dependency was low, and considering her advanced age and comorbidities, device retrieval or reimplantation was not performed. Although leadless pacemakers reduce complications associated with conventional transvenous systems, device-specific mechanical complications have been reported. We present a rare case of tine fracture of a Micra™ AV2 device resulting in migration into the pulmonary artery. Learning objective Tine fracture is a rare but potentially serious mechanical complication of leadless pacemakers. When pacing thresholds increase or pacing failure occurs, careful assessment of device position and fixation, including detailed imaging review, is essential.

warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry. Over-drainage is siphon-driven; without a hydrostatic column, it may not occur.

informational.mechanism: Flow reversal obstruction clearing (R3)
informational.lesson: Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: A 78-year-old male with a history of ischemic heart disease with prior myocardial infarction, severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and a device-related implantable cardioverter defibrillator (DR ICD) was admitted following a road traffic accident due to a sudden loss of control of the vehicle following a syncope. Initial investigations ruled out acute coronary syndrome and did not point to neurological causes. Device interrogation revealed the presence of pacemaker-mediated tachycardia (PMT), but since the episode trigger had been programmed off, it was not possible to determine when they occurred, how long they lasted, or their rate. However, atrial threshold testing promptly provoked a PMT. The induced PMT led to a tachycardia of 130 bpm, causing severe symptomatic hypotension with a mean blood pressure falling below 50 mmHg. This could be easily reproduced several times. Given the patient's severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction and the absence of any overt alternative explanation, the PMT likely triggered the syncope preceding the car accident. Management focused on reprogramming the DR ICD. The most critical adaptation was a mode switch from DDD to DDIR to prevent atrial tracking, effectively terminating PMT episodes. A prolongation of the postventricular atrial refractory period (PVARP) was not possible due to the very slow VA conduction. The follow-up revealed no other episodes of PMT and the patient no longer experiences episodes of presyncope or syncope. This report highlights the potential for PMTs to induce severe hemodynamic instability and syncope, underscoring the importance of meticulous device evaluation.

custody_records.raw_content: Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) is a reversible form of acute cardiac syndrome usually arising in response to various emotional and physical stressors. TTS due to cardiac pacing has been an uncommon phenomenon mostly attributable to a variety of periprocedural conventional stressors including anxiety, pain and low cardiac output. Interestingly, intraventricular mechanical factors might also play a pivotal role in TTS evolution due to cardiac pacing. Notably, this phenomenon may be potentially underdiagnosed due to a variety of factors including atypical symptoms and masked electrocardiographic (ECG) changes potentially suggesting its higher incidence in clinical practice.The present paper aims to focus on mechanistic and clinical implications of TTS due to cardiac pacing procedures including conventional permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and conduction system pacing (CSP) along with a particular emphasis on intraventricular mechanical factors as potential TTS triggers in this context.

custody_records.raw_content: Bradycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is a reversible form of myocardial dysfunction caused by prolonged bradyarrhythmia, most commonly due to high-grade atrioventricular block or sinus node dysfunction. Although bradycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is well recognized in human medicine, it remains underreported in veterinary literature. This case series describes 3 dogs diagnosed with 3rd-degree atrioventricular block that presented with clinical signs including exercise intolerance, syncope, and cardiomegaly. Each dog underwent comprehensive diagnostic evaluation, including physical examination, thoracic radiography, echocardiography, and electrocardiography. Bradycardia-induced transient myocardial dysfunction was suspected, based on the presence of bradyarrhythmia in conjunction with cardiac enlargement and preserved systolic function. All dogs were treated with permanent pacemaker implantation. Postoperative follow-ups documented marked clinical improvement, with resolution of exercise intolerance or syncope. Radiographic and echocardiographic reassessments demonstrated reductions in atrial and ventricular internal dimensions, supporting the reversibility of myocardial remodeling once normal heart rate was restored. No major complications were observed during follow-up periods that ranged from several months to > 4 y. Key clinical message: These findings supported the presence of bradycardia-induced transient myocardial dysfunction in dogs and underscored the importance of recognizing bradyarrhythmia as a potentially reversible cause of cardiomyopathy. Early diagnosis and timely pacemaker implantation can result in substantial clinical and structural cardiac recovery.

custody_records.raw_content: A 96-year-old woman underwent implantation of a leadless pacemaker (Micra™ AV2; Medtronic, Inc., Minneapolis, MN, USA) for sick sinus syndrome. One month after implantation, pacing failure due to an elevated pacing threshold was observed, and the pacing output was increased. At routine follow-up one year after implantation, recurrent pacing failure was detected. Chest radiography revealed migration of the device into the left pulmonary artery. At least two of the four fixation tines were missing from the device body, and one fractured tine remained embedded in the right ventricular myocardium. Because the patient was asymptomatic, ventricular pacing dependency was low, and considering her advanced age and comorbidities, device retrieval or reimplantation was not performed. Although leadless pacemakers reduce complications associated with conventional transvenous systems, device-specific mechanical complications have been reported. We present a rare case of tine fracture of a Micra™ AV2 device resulting in migration into the pulmonary artery. Learning objective Tine fracture is a rare but potentially serious mechanical complication of leadless pacemakers. When pacing thresholds increase or pacing failure occurs, careful assessment of device position and fixation, including detailed imaging review, is essential.
